data.title: Skalica – the Hradisko hillfort on Kalvária hill
data.excerpt: On the hill with the calvary above the north-western edge of old Skalica lay an elliptical fortified enclosure about 120 × 40–50 m in size, protected by a massive rampart and a deep ditch; its eastern part is crowned by the Romanesque rotunda of St George, still the symbol of the town. The grave of an Old Hungarian warrior was found in the slope of the hill, and 1,392 silver coins came to light during ploughing in 1958.

children.text: The Skalica hillfort lies in the immediate vicinity of the north-western edge of the old town. It consists of two larger rises, separated from one another by a pronounced cut on the ground which today forms part of the road leading to the town centre. A fortified enclosure of elliptical shape was situated on a natural elevation that runs westwards into the inundation area of the Morava, rising as much as 20 m above the river floodplain and 6–8 m above the level of the terrain on the eastern side; its longer axis is oriented NW–SE, with a length of about 120 m and a width of about 40–50 m. The remains of a wide ditch, evidently much deformed by later interventions and discernible around Kalvária on the western, northern and southern sides, appear to belong to this phase. The hillfort was protected by a massive rampart and a deep ditch. A timber palisade has to be assumed on the crest of the rampart. The second, smaller part is formed by a sloping area on the eastern side measuring about 82 m × 17 m, on top of which stands the Romanesque rotunda that remains the symbol of Skalica to this day and that probably already served the owner of the hillfort in the High Middle Ages.

children.text: As part of his topography of Skalica, F. V. Sasinek dealt intensively with the origin and the location of the original castle, which stood on the hill with the calvary and formed the nucleus of the later fortified town. The author relies on toponymy. In charters of 1648 and 1753 he found that the hill was already called Hradisko at that time. Following this name, Sasinek searched for the remains of a masonry medieval castle. When he did not find them, he concluded that there must have been a prehistoric settlement fortified with ramparts on the hill.

In the name Hradisko, which denotes the south-eastern spur of the calvary hill, a precious toponymic document has survived to the present day, one on which a historian can safely rely. Places bearing names such as Hrádok, Zámčisko, Pohanský vrch, Zemný hrad, Valy or Stráža are almost always either prehistoric, protohistoric or medieval fortified settlements. There is no reason to doubt the value and significance of such toponymic evidence precisely in the case of Skalica, which lies in a zone of very dense Slavic occupation. The name Hradisko, which was preserved in the memory of the local population, may have referred to a vanished prehistoric fort, originally perhaps as early as the Bronze Age or the Hallstatt period. From the periods mentioned (the Bronze Age) we know several interesting finds from Skalica, such as a bronze knife, a neck ring or pottery. The well-known Slavic barrow cemetery not far from Skalica testifies to the presence of a Great Moravian elite, which as a rule used to inhabit fortified places. In this case the hillfort may have been taken over by the first Slavic settlers living in the district of Skalica, who, when they arrived, found on the hill only the ruins of a settlement twelve to fifteen centuries old. We do not know, however, whether the term hrad or hradisko already existed in the language of the Great Moravian or still older Slavs. It is therefore perhaps more accurate to hold that the name Hradisko came into being only at the time when the first town walls of Skalica were being built, when the inhabitants were leaving the older castle part of the town on the calvary hill and occupying a larger area.

children.text: Janšák states that the terrain relief of the hill with the calvary is the weightiest evidence for the location of the castle on the area that until recently was called Hradisko. Along its entire circumference it slopes very gently towards the adjacent plain. Only to the north-east of the rotunda of St George is there an abrupt step, formed by a harder rock substratum. If we disregard the section of the town walls whose band descends from the rotunda towards the north-east, and if we were to remove all the dwelling houses and farm buildings that are attached to the walls on both sides, a steep promontory-like spur 8 to 10 m high would appear. And the hill has retained this height even after all the levelling and grading works to which it was subjected over the centuries, especially during the construction of the walls. On the southern, eastern and north-eastern sides of this step there were marshes formed by the Zlatnícky brook. Along the whole circumference of the hill with the calvary and the cemeteries there was no more suitable place, either in prehistory or in the early Middle Ages, for establishing a fortified settlement or for building a small fort. All the factors needed for the safety of the fort were concentrated here: an elevated promontory-like spur and a wide and deep marsh at its foot – natural protection on three sides. Only here could an earthen fort defended by ramparts have stood, and the later timber fortress after which the place received the name Hradisko, while the rest of the surface of the calvary hill remained without a name.

children.text: The results of the archaeological excavation carried out so far suggest that the existence of a castle in Skalica can probably be reckoned with from about the turn of the 12th and 13th centuries. The rotunda served as a proprietary church with a small area for burials. Alexander Ruttkay is of the opinion that this was not an earthen fort – a hillfort – but a feature fortified probably with a stone wall and a ditch, and that it came to an end as a result of the construction of the town walls after 1372. The ditch which today separates the small fort from the western spur of the elevation with the rotunda was evidently present at that spot in the Middle Ages as well, first as a wide ditch adjoining the town wall, and subsequently it was widened for the road that today forms the axis of the street between Kalvária and the rotunda of St George. The present height of the Kalvária rise does not correspond to the situation in the Middle Ages. In her description of the Old Hungarian grave in the slope of Kalvária, L. Kraskovská reports that beneath the surface humus there was a fill of yellow sandy clay about 2.5 m thick, which she dates to the 18th century; beneath this layer, that is at a depth of 2.5 m, there were two thin layers containing “ash, charcoal and…sherds…of the 14th and 15th centuries”. In the second medieval layer there was a “stone floor of sandstone, and on it…a layer of fired dark grey clay…” with a screed described as “pink plaster”. The Old Hungarian grave was recorded at a depth of about 1.5 m below the level of the first medieval layer. The excavation of the surroundings of the rotunda in 2005 also confirmed that the present height level of the summit area of the hillfort does not agree with the original medieval one, and that during the Late Middle Ages and the modern period it was evidently raised in various ways. This is also one of the reasons why it is difficult to find pottery, for instance, on the hillfort, since the medieval layer lies at a considerable depth. Any older layers must therefore be expected deeper still. The excavation in 2005 also confirmed that in the Middle Ages the rotunda stood inside the town fortification.

children.text: Rudolf Hikl, who studied the hillfort in Skalica after Sasinek, states that in his view the small fort was built by the counts of Pezinok, from 1217 until the end of the 13th century the owners of Skalica, which had been granted to them by the Hungarian kings Andrew II and Béla IV. The fort is said to have been of timber and to have been the seat of the ruling landlords. In its vicinity, however, they built the stone church of St George in the form of a rotunda, whose basic architectural character has survived to this day. As early as the beginning of the 13th century the confinium (border zone) became part of the estates of the nobility. If we take into account that the task of the lords of Pezinok and Svätý Jur was not only further settlement but undoubtedly also care for the protection of the frontier, the assumption arises that the first phase of the fortified residence with the proprietary rotunda in Skalica is connected with their activity. The further development, however, is unclear. After 1250 the castles of Holíč, Branč and Senica came to the fore in the neighbourhood of Skalica.

children.text: During the existence of the church and the small fort, a suburbium developed in their neighbourhood on the south-eastern slope of the hill; it had the character of an agricultural settlement, which was common in the Middle Ages. The settlers of the suburbium, however, did not build their dwellings on the hill but came down from it to the water, which was the decisive factor in choosing the site for newly built cottages. In this way an agglomeration of dwellings arose, at first only in the immediate neighbourhood of the church, where Podhradie and Blahova street are today. Later the settlement expanded over the area occupied by the old part of the town, enclosed by walls. Two brooks, the Zlatnícky and the Stračinský, favoured this development by their position and by their volume of water, distributed evenly throughout the year. The shape of the terrain, closed in by the two brooks, also had a favourable effect. Both these factors determined the choice of the position and the course of the walls when, at the end of the 14th century, a settlement accessible from all sides became an enclosed town girdled by masonry walls. An interesting piece of evidence for the existence of the hillfort is

, said to be kept in the archive in Brno and to have been made around the year 1500. The map is supposed to show Skalica at the time of King Sigismund’s stay at the castle. According to the map, the castle was linked to the rotunda and the cemetery by a drawbridge over a water-filled moat.

children.text: From the cadastral area of Skalica we know interesting archaeological finds dating from as early as the Stone Age, through the Bronze Age and the Roman period. Well known is the Skalica barrow cemetery of the Great Moravian period, which lies in the locality known as Kopečnice and which contained exceptionally rich grave goods, both of women (rich jewellery) and of men (swords, other weapons). The barrow cemetery shows that a Great Moravian elite lived in the territory of Skalica in the 9th century. The hillfort could therefore have been in use as early as the Great Moravian period, but because of the absence of more comprehensive archaeological excavation we have no evidence as yet for this logical assumption. It would also be suggested by the find of the grave of a 10th-century Old Hungarian warrior near the hillfort, which may be connected with the period of alternating conflicts and alliances between the Great Moravians and the Old Hungarians. I regard the find of 1,392 silver coins, among which 13th-century Viennese pfennigs predominated, as a very interesting numismatic discovery. It was found during ploughing in 1958, the coins having been deposited in a pottery vessel. The coins could perhaps be connected with the Mongol invasion of the Kingdom of Hungary, in which case it may be assumed that they were hidden by one of the wealthy inhabitants of Skalica out of fear of these nomads. With a little imagination it may be supposed that the hoard belonged to one of the counts of Svätý Jur and Pezinok, to whom Hikl attributes the building of the Skalica hillfort.
